title: Structures of sin (1987)
hookLine: sin can be built into systems

lines: NO ADDRESS, NO ID, NO BED.
NOBODY IN THE ROOM IS CRUEL.
cards: A man at a counter needs a bed for the night. The shelter needs to see an ID. The office that issues IDs needs a home address.
He has no home address; that's why he's at the shelter. The clerk is polite. The man in line behind him is patient.
Nobody in the room means him any harm, and still the door stays shut, the same way, for the next person too. Something is wrong, and it isn't sitting in any one heart in that room.
It's built into the way things are set up. Today's word gives it a name: structures of sin.

teach.h: HARM BUILT INTO HOW THINGS ARE SET UP.
teach.b: First, the name. John Paul the Second used the phrase in a letter on social concern, Sollicitudo Rei Socialis.

He meant habits, rules and arrangements in a society that keep producing harm, even when no one in particular is choosing harm today. Second, where they come from. These structures don't fall from the sky.

They are rooted in personal sin, and always linked to the concrete choices of people: those who set them up, strengthen them, and make them hard to take apart. Once built, they spread, and become the soil for more sin.
The Catechism says it in one breath: structures of sin are the expression and the effect of personal sins. Third, what feeds them.

teach.h: PROFIT AND POWER AT ANY PRICE.
teach.b: The letter names two attitudes: an all-consuming desire for profit, and a thirst for power that wants to impose its will on others, both at any price. Neither needs a villain twirling a mustache.
A lot of ordinary people quietly sharing them is enough. Fourth, an old insight.

teach.h: WOE TO THEM THAT MAKE WICKED LAWS.
teach.b: The prophet Isaiah saw it, in the Douay-Rheims: "Woe to them that make wicked laws: and when they write, write injustice." Sin can be written down, filed and stamped. The teaching cuts both ways.

A system doesn't excuse anyone's own choices. And being personally kind doesn't excuse ignoring the system. The letter's answer is conversion, and the solidarity from last week: a firm commitment to the good of all.

how: Catholics examine structures of sin in social-justice education, in parish advocacy on laws and policies, and sometimes in examinations of conscience that ask about a person's part in unjust systems as well as personal sins.

games.q: you're the polite clerk. the rule keeps sending the same kind of person away. what does the teaching on structures of sin say?
o: it's only the rule's fault, so it isn't your concern.
the harm is real, rooted in human choices, and you can help change it.
nothing can be done about systems.
games.why: the letter roots structures of sin in personal choices: people build them, strengthen them, and can help take them apart.

practice: Think through a normal day, a form you filled in, a line you stood in, a rule at work or school, and look for one place where the setup itself keeps hurting the same kind of people, whoever is on duty.
Don't try to fix it; just see it clearly, then ask the harder question: where am I part of it, even a little, and where could I push back? If you pray, bring both to God.

wordCard.voice: Structures of sin. Ways a society is set up that keep producing harm, rooted in personal choices, fed by profit and power at any price. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: sin in systems. The wrong was built in. I'll be here tomorrow.
